danish.title: Tiende bog (1812) — Kapitel 27
paragraphs: Den 25. august tilbragte Napoleon, ifølge sine historikere, hele dagen til hest med at inspicere terrænet, vurdere de planer, hans marskalker forelagde ham, og personligt udstede ordrer til sine generaler.

Den russiske hærs oprindelige linje langs floden Kolotsja var blevet forskudt af erobringen af Sjevardino-redouten den 24., og en del af linjen — venstre fløj — var trukket tilbage. Denne del var ikke befæstet, ikke længere beskyttet af floden, og foran den lå det mest åbne og jævne terræn. Det stod klart for enhver — militær som civil — at det var her, de franske måtte angribe. Det krævede ingen genial indsigt at se det, ingen af de foranstaltninger og overvejelser, som Napoleon og hans marskalker brugte tid på, og der var slet ikke behov for den særlige evne kaldet geni, som så beredvilligt tilskrives Napoleon. Men de historikere, der siden beskrev begivenheden, de mænd, der dengang omgav Napoleon, og han selv var af en anden mening.

Napoleon red hen over sletten og inspicerede terrænet med en alvorlig mine og i tavshed, nikkede anerkendende eller rystede tvivlende på hovedet, og uden at meddele generalerne omkring sig den dybe tankegang, der styrede hans beslutninger, gav han blot sine endelige afgørelser. Da han lyttede til en ide fra general Davout (Hertug af Eckmühl) om at omgå russernes venstre fløj, sagde Napoleon, at det ikke var nødvendigt — uden at forklare hvorfor. Til general Compans' forslag om at føre sin division gennem skoven svarede han derimod med samtykke, skønt den såkaldte Hertug af Elchingen — det vil sige Ney — tillod sig at bemærke, at en fremrykning gennem skoven var risikabel og kunne sprede divisionen.

Efter at have inspiceret terrænet ud for Sjevardino-redouten overvejede Napoleon stilfærdigt et øjeblik og udpegede derefter de steder, hvor to batterier skulle opstilles den følgende dag for at beskyde de russiske stillinger. Han beordrede også, at et artillerianlæg skulle placeres dér for at åbne ild mod det russiske feltværk.
Efter at have givet disse og andre ordrer vendte han tilbage til sit telt, og slagdispositionerne blev skrevet ned efter hans diktat.
Disse dispositioner, som franske historikere skriver om med begejstring og andre historikere med dyb respekt, lød som følger:
Ved daggry skal de to nye batterier, der er opstillet i nattens løb på den slette, som Hertugen af Eckmühl besætter, åbne ild mod fjendens modstående batterier.

Samtidig skal kommandanten for Første Korps' artilleri, general Pernetti, med tredive kanoner fra Campans division og alle haubitser fra Dessaix' og Friants divisioner rykke frem og åbne kraftig ild mod fjendens feltværk.
24 kanoner fra gardeartilleriet, 30 kanoner fra Campans division
og 8 kanoner fra Friants og Dessaix' divisioner —
i alt 62 kanoner.

Kommandanten for Tredje Korps' artilleri, general Fouché, skal placere haubitserne fra Tredje og Ottende Korps, seksten i alt, på flankerne af det batteri, der skal bombardere det venstre feltværk, hvilket giver i alt fyrre kanoner rettet mod dette.
General Sorbier skal være klar til ved første ordre at rykke frem med alle gardeartilleriets haubitser mod det ene eller det andet feltværk.
Under bombardementet skal Fyrst Poniatowski rykke frem gennem skoven mod landsbyen og vende fjendens position.
General Campan skal rykke gennem skoven for at erobre den første befæstning.
Når fremrykningen er begyndt på denne måde, vil ordrer blive givet i overensstemmelse med fjendens bevægelser.

Bombardementet på venstre fløj skal begynde, så snart kanonerne fra højre fløj høres. Skarpskytte fra Morands division og Vicekongens division skal åbne kraftig ild, når de ser, at angreb fra højre fløj er i gang.

Vicekongen skal besætte landsbyen og krydse ved dens tre broer og derefter rykke frem til de samme højder som Morands og Gibrards divisioner, som under hans ledelse skal rettes mod redouten og gå i linje med de øvrige tropper.
Alt dette skal ske i god orden (le tout se fera avec ordre et méthode), så vidt muligt under bevarelse af tropper i reserve.
Det kejserlige hovedkvarter nær Mozhajsk,
den 6. september 1812.

Disse dispositioner, som er yderst uklare og forvirrede, hvis man tillader sig at betragte arrangementerne uden religiøs ærefrygt for hans geni, handlede om Napoleons ordrer vedrørende fire punkter — fire angreb. Ingen af disse ordrer blev udført, og ingen af dem kunne udføres.

I dispositionen siges det først, at batterierne placeret på den af Napoleon valgte plads, sammen med Pernettis og Fouchés kanoner — i alt 102 stykker — skulle åbne ild og overdænge de russiske befæstninger med granater. Men dette kunne ikke gennemføres, for fra de af Napoleon udpegede positioner nåede granaterne ikke russerne, og de 102 kanoner skød forgæves, indtil den nærmeste kommandant på eget initiativ rykkede dem nærmere frem — uden ordrer.

Den anden ordre var, at Poniatowski, der rykkede mod landsbyen gennem skoven, skulle vende den russiske venstre fløj. Det kunne ikke gøres, og det blev ikke gjort, for Poniatowski blev, da han rykkede frem mod landsbyen, mødt af Tutsjkov, der spærrede hans vej. Han kunne aldrig, og gjorde aldrig, den manøvre, som var tiltænkt ham.

Den tredje ordre lød: General Campan skal rykke gennem skoven for at erobre den første befæstning. Campans division erobrede ikke den første befæstning, men blev drevet tilbage, for da den trådte ud af skoven, blev den nødt til at omgruppere under granatild — noget Napoleon ikke vidste.

Den fjerde ordre lød: Vicekongen skal besætte landsbyen (Borodino) og krydse ved dens tre broer og derefter rykke frem til de samme højder som Morands og Gérards divisioner (for hvis bevægelser der ikke var givet nogen retningslinjer) og sammen med dem slutte op mod redouten.

Så vidt man kan forstå — ikke så meget ud fra denne uforståelige sætning som af de forsøg, Vicekongen gjorde på at udføre de ordrer, han havde fået — skulle han rykke frem fra venstre gennem Borodino mod redouten, mens divisionerne fra Morand og Gérard samtidig rykkede fremad fra front. Men det fremgår ikke, og den ringe klarhed i ordren gjorde, at det var umuligt at afgøre, hvornår eller ad hvilken vej disse divisioner skulle rykke frem.

Alt dette kunne ikke og blev ikke udført, ligesom de øvrige dele af dispositionen. Vicekongen blev efter at have passeret Borodino drevet tilbage til Kolotsja og kunne ikke komme videre; mens Morands og Gérards divisioner ikke indtog redouten, men blev slået tilbage, og redouten blev først erobret sidst på dagen af kavaleri — et resultat, som Napoleon formentlig hverken havde forudset eller hørt om. Ikke en eneste ordre i slagplanen blev altså udført eller kunne være blevet det. Nu står der ganske vist i planen, at så snart kampen er indledt på denne måde, vil der blive givet ordrer efter fjendens bevægelser. Man kunne da tro, at Napoleon under slaget ville træffe alle de nødvendige forholdsregler. Men det gjorde han ikke og kunne han ikke gøre. Under hele slaget var han så langt borte, at han, som det senere viste sig, umuligt kunne vide, hvordan det gik, og ikke én af hans ordrer under kampen lod sig udføre.

english.title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 27
paragraphs: On the twenty-fifth of August, so his historians tell us, Napoleon spent the entire day on horseback, inspecting the terrain, considering plans submitted by his marshals, and personally giving orders to his generals.

The original Russian line along the river Kolocha had been disrupted by the capture of the Shevardino Redoubt on the twenty-fourth, and part of the line—the left flank—had been pulled back. That part was not entrenched, and in front of it the ground was more open and level than elsewhere. It was obvious to anyone, military or civilian, that this was where the French should attack. It would seem that no great deliberation was needed to reach this conclusion, nor any special effort on the part of the Emperor and his marshals, nor any need for that supreme quality called genius which people are so ready to attribute to Napoleon; yet the historians who described the event later, and the men who surrounded Napoleon at the time, and Napoleon himself, all thought otherwise.

Napoleon rode across the plain, surveyed the terrain with a profound air and in silence, nodded approvingly or shook his head dubiously, and without explaining to the generals around him the deep course of reasoning behind his decisions, merely gave them his final conclusions as commands. Having heard a suggestion from Davout (now called the Prince of Eckmuhl) to turn the Russian left wing, Napoleon said it should not be done, without explaining why. To a proposal by General Campan (who was to attack the fleches) to lead his division through the woods, Napoleon agreed, though the so-called Duke of Elchingen (Ney) ventured to remark that a move through the woods was dangerous and might throw the division into disorder.

After inspecting the terrain opposite the Shevardino Redoubt, Napoleon pondered briefly in silence and then indicated where two batteries should be placed by the next morning to act against the Russian entrenchments, and where the field artillery should be positioned in line with them.
After giving these and other orders, he returned to his tent, and the battle plan was written down from his dictation.
These dispositions, which French historians write about with enthusiasm and other historians with deep respect, were as follows:
At dawn the two new batteries established during the night on the plain occupied by the Prince of Eckmuhl will open fire on the opposing batteries of the enemy.

At the same time the commander of the artillery of the 1st Corps, General Pernetti, with thirty cannon of Campan's division and all the howitzers of Dessaix's and Friant's divisions, will move forward, open fire, and bombard the enemy's battery, against which will operate:
24 guns of the Guard artillery, 30 guns of Campan's division,
and 8 guns of Friant's and Dessaix's divisions—
in all 62 guns.

The commander of the artillery of the 3rd Corps, General Fouche, will place the howitzers of the 3rd and 8th Corps, sixteen in all, on the flanks of the battery that is to bombard the entrenchment on the left, which will have forty guns in all directed against it.
General Sorbier must be ready at the first order to advance with all the howitzers of the Guard artillery against either entrenchment.
During the cannonade, Prince Poniatowski is to advance through the wood on the village and turn the enemy's position.
General Campan will move through the wood to seize the first fortification.
After the advance has begun in this manner, orders will be given in accordance with the enemy's movements.

The cannonade on the left flank will begin as soon as the guns on the right wing are heard. The sharpshooters of Morand's division and of the Viceroy's division will open heavy fire when they see the attack begin on the right wing.

The Viceroy will occupy the village and cross by its three bridges, advancing to the same heights as Morand's and Gerard's divisions, which under his command will be directed against the redoubt and fall into line with the rest of the forces.
All this must be done in good order, retaining troops in reserve as far as possible.
The Imperial Camp near Mozhaysk,
September 6, 1812.

These dispositions, which are very vague and confused if one allows oneself to regard the arrangements without religious awe of Napoleon's genius, consisted of four directives—four different orders. Not one of them was, or could be, carried out.

The dispositions say first that the batteries placed at the spot Napoleon chose, together with Pernetti's and Fouche's guns (102 in all), were to open fire and bombard the Russian fleches and redoubts. This could not be done, because from the spots Napoleon selected, the shells could not reach the Russian works, and those 102 guns fired into the air until the nearest commander, contrary to Napoleon's instructions, moved them forward.

The second order was that Poniatowski, advancing on the village through the wood, should turn the Russian left flank. This could not be done and was not done, because Poniatowski, advancing through the wood, met Tuchkov there blocking his way, and could not and did not turn the Russian position.

The third order was: General Campan will move through the wood to seize the first fortification. Campan's division did not seize the first fortification but was driven back, because on emerging from the wood it had to re-form under grapeshot—something Napoleon hadn't foreseen.

The fourth order was: The Viceroy will occupy the village (Borodino) and cross by its three bridges, advancing to the same heights as Morand's and Gerard's divisions (for whose movements no directions are given), which under his command will be directed against the redoubt and fall into line with the rest of the forces.

As far as one can make out—not so much from this unintelligible sentence as from the Viceroy's attempts to execute it—he was to advance from the left through Borodino to the redoubt while Morand's and Gerard's divisions advanced simultaneously from the front.

All of this, like the rest of the plan, was not and could not be executed. After passing through Borodino, the Viceroy was driven back to the Kolocha and could get no farther; while Morand's and Gerard's divisions did not take the redoubt but were beaten back, and the redoubt was only captured at the end of the battle by cavalry (something probably unforeseen and unheard of by Napoleon). So not a single order in the plan was, or could be, carried out. But the dispositions state that after the fight begins in this manner, orders will be given according to the enemy's movements—and so it might be supposed that Napoleon would make all necessary adjustments during the battle. But this was not and could not be done, because throughout the entire battle Napoleon was so far away that (as later became clear) he could not follow the battle's progress, and not one of his orders during the fight could be carried out.
